## Source and status

Every parameter in this tool comes from one published, openly licensed study:

> Palacios A, Espinola N, Gonzalez JM, Rojas-Roque C, Rivas MM, Kanevski D, Morisset P,
> Augustovski F, Pichon-Riviere A, Bardach A. **Budget impact analysis of venetoclax for the
> management of acute myeloid leukemia from the perspective of the social security and the
> private sector in Argentina.** *PLoS One*. 2024;19(1):e0295798.
> [doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0295798](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0295798) — CC-BY 4.0.

This is a **methods demonstration**, not a client deliverable, not a validated reimbursement
model, and not a pricing recommendation. It contains no confidential or commercial data.
Market shares in the source are projections supplied by the manufacturer and validated by a
Delphi panel of six onco-haematologists; they are not observed market data.

Every input carries a source tag — a table number, a stated derivation, or an explicit
assumption. There are three assumptions and they are labelled as such.
:::

## What a budget impact model actually is

A cost-effectiveness model asks whether a therapy is worth its price. A budget impact model
asks a narrower and more immediate question: **can this payer afford to adopt it, and when
does the money move?**

The answer is a subtraction:

> the world **with** the new therapy, minus the world **without** it

That subtraction is the whole model. It is also where most of the difficulty sits, because the
two worlds must be built on the same population, the same time horizon and the same cost
categories, and only then differenced. Without an explicit market share layer there is only one
world and no budget impact at all — which is why that layer, not the headline number, is the
part worth inspecting first.

## The rebuild

The tool below reconstructs the published model from its parameters rather than restating its
results. Seven layers, in the order a reviewer would work through them:

1. the **epidemiology funnel**, from covered lives to treatable patients
2. **market share** in both worlds, year by year — the layer that makes it a budget impact model
3. **cost per patient per year**, in six components, built bottom-up
4. **budget impact**, annual and cumulative, with per-member-per-month
5. **one-way sensitivity analysis**, against the published tornado
6. **reconciliation** with the published results, including where it does not agree
7. **provenance** for every parameter

Three things surfaced during the rebuild that are worth naming, because they are the parts a
spreadsheet would hide:

- **The published supplement contradicts itself.** S1 Table and S7 Table assign the venetoclax +
  decitabine and venetoclax + LDAC market shares in opposite order. Reconciling each against the
  drug costs in Table 4 settles it, and the model follows the assignment that reproduces the
  published spend.
- **Drug cost had to be rebuilt as a function of treatment duration**, not taken as a fixed annual
  total. Duration is the leading sensitivity driver in the source; with a frozen annual cost it
  cannot move the result at all, and the sensitivity analysis would be theatre.
- **The mechanism behind hospitalisation is in the questionnaire, not the paper.** The main text
  never says how hospital days are derived. The Delphi questionnaire in the supplementary material
  asks the panel for days per cycle separately for patients who do and do not achieve complete
  remission, on the stated assumption that failing to reach remission means progression, and
  progression means admissions. So the headline clinical result reaches the budget through hospital
  days. An earlier version of this rebuild drove hospitalisation from time to blood count recovery
  instead — an invention with no documentary basis, which left the component at less than half the
  published figure.
- **Two kinds of calibration, and only one of them is legitimate.** Scaling whole cost components
  to match published levels was tested and rejected: it distorts the difference between the two
  worlds, which is the only quantity a budget impact model reports. Estimating individual
  parameters the source uses but never publishes — the panel's returned hospital days, the
  effective duration of transfusion independence — against all the published totals including the
  difference is a different thing, and it is what the rebuild does. The estimates land close to the
  questionnaire's own suggested values, which a wrong structure would not produce.

## Technical notes

The tool is a static page: three JavaScript files, no server, no build step, no dependencies.
The separation is deliberate and is part of the point.

- `bim_params.js` — every parameter, each with a source tag. No logic.
- `bim_engine.js` — pure calculation. No DOM, no globals, parameters passed in, so the
  sensitivity analysis perturbs a copy rather than the base case.
- `bim_ui.js` — rendering and event binding only.

A reviewer who wants to audit the model does not need to read the interface code. They open the
parameter file and check it against the paper — which is the same thing they would ask to do
with a spreadsheet, and rarely can.

## Limitations

### The population is a flow, not a stock

This is the limitation that matters most, and it is one the source does not list.

The model carries no population *stock*. Each budget year is an independent cohort of newly
diagnosed patients — 129 of them, the same number every year — and every patient is costed for
exactly one year before leaving the model. The arithmetic is explicit: active treatment plus the
post-active period always sum to 13.04 cycles, which is 365 days. Nobody carries over. The
entire growth in spending across the horizon comes from the treatment mix shifting toward
venetoclax, not from patients accumulating.

Three consequences follow, and a payer will find all three.

**Incidence rather than prevalence is right here, but the source says the wrong word.** This is
first-line treatment of newly diagnosed disease, so only incident patients are eligible; counting
prevalent patients would double-count people already treated. The source nevertheless writes that
it assumes "the prevalence of AML is constant", while the parameter it uses is an incidence rate.
The distinction matters elsewhere: for a chronic therapy the treated pool accumulates year on
year, and an incidence-only model would badly understate later years. In unfit AML, with median
survival around ten to fifteen months, almost nothing accumulates.

**Survival gain does not feed back into the population.** Venetoclax combinations extend overall
survival materially. Both worlds nonetheless contain the same 129 patients, each alive and
incurring a full year of costs. Mortality is absent from both arms, so the model cannot express
the argument a payer will certainly make — that a therapy which keeps people alive creates
patients who go on costing money. Because the comparator arm has the worse survival, holding
everyone alive for a full year overstates the comparator's cost more than venetoclax's, which
compresses the difference between the two worlds.

**Costs are assigned to the year of diagnosis, not the year they fall.** The source acknowledges
this one: in practice, patients responding well continue therapy beyond the budget period.
Venetoclax regimens run longer than their comparators — 10.98 cycles against 8.8 for azacitidine
and 3.76 for low-dose cytarabine — so they spill across year boundaries more. Charging each
cohort's whole cost to its year of diagnosis therefore flattens the ramp: the real budget
pressure is more back-loaded than the model shows. This is the difference between costing each
incident cohort in full and costing only what falls inside the budget year, and it is the second
that answers a payer's cash-flow question.

The **eligible population growth** control is the one extension beyond the source. At its default
of 0% the model reproduces the publication exactly. It is worth having because the ISPOR budget
impact guidance the source itself cites asks that the changing size and composition of the
population be reflected, and here the entire target population sits in the 65+ segment, which
grows faster than the membership containing it. Growth is applied to the eligible population
rather than to membership deliberately: membership is a normalising convention, and growing it
would scale the budget and the per-member denominator together, leaving PMPM unchanged.

### Scope held to the source

Three years, 28-day cycles, deterministic, no probabilistic sensitivity analysis. No QALYs or
ICERs — this is a budget impact model, and mixing the two questions is a common way of answering
neither. Costs are US dollars at 2020 prices with no inflation adjustment, following the source's
stated reasoning for excluding it under high inflation.

### What reconciles, and what does not

Drug acquisition, adverse events, hospitalisation and transfusions rebuild to within 0.3% of the
published figures, and the year-3 budget impact lands within 0.1% under both payer perspectives.
Two components do not. Administration is about 45% low, because the source costs later-cycle
administration at a daily hospital stay whose unit cost it never reports. Monitoring is about 12%
low for reasons not traceable to any published quantity. Together they are 0.5% of total spend.
Both are shown in the reconciliation panel rather than closed by fitting — the distinction being
that estimating an unpublished parameter inside a documented structure is legitimate, while scaling
a component until the total agrees is not.
